3288.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
3288.text: In which of the following, elements are correctly arranged in the decreasing order of their second ionisation enthalpies?
3288.sol: As we move across a period, effective nuclear charge $\left(Z_{\text{eff }}\right)$ increases and so do the first ionisation energy, $\mathrm{F} \gt \mathrm{O} \gt \mathrm{N} \gt \mathrm{C}. So, the correct order of second ionisation potential is \mathrm{O}$ \gt $\mathrm{F}$ \gt $\mathrm{N}$ \gt $\mathrm{C}$.

5227.text: At \(300 $\mathrm{ K}$\) an ideal solution is formed by mixing \(460 $\mathrm{ g}$\) of toluene with \(390 $\mathrm{ g}$\) benzene. If the vapour pressure of pure toluene and benzene at \(300 $\mathrm{ K}$\) are 32 and \(40 $\mathrm{ mm}$\) respectively, the mole fraction of toluene in vapour phase is
5227.sol:
Given, \(w_a=460 \mathrm{ g}\) (toluene)
\(w_B=390 \mathrm{ g} \text{ (benzene) }\)
Vapour pressure of pure toluene \($\left(p_A\right)=32 \mathrm{ mm}\)
Vapour pressure of pure benzene \(\left(p_B\right)=40 \mathrm{ mm}\)
Moles of toluene, \(\left(n_A\right)=\frac{w_A}{M_A}=\frac{460}{92}\)
Moles of benzene, \(n_B=\frac{w_B}{M_B}=\frac{390}{78}\)
Hence, mole fraction of toluene \(\chi_A\).
\(\chi_A=\frac{\frac{460}{92}}{\frac{460}{92}+\frac{390}{78}}\)
Mole fraction of benzene \(\left(\chi_B\right)\)
\begin{gathered}
\chi_$ B=$\frac{$\frac{390}{78}$$}{$\frac{460}{92}+\frac{390}{78}$$}$\\
\therefore \quad p_{$\text{total }$}=p^{{}^{\circ}}{ }_A \chi_A+p^{{}^{\circ}}{ }_B \chi_B \\
p_{$\text{total }$}=32 $\times\left(\frac{\frac{460}{92}$}{$\frac{460}{92}+\frac{390}{78}$}\right)+40$\left(\frac{\frac{390}{78}$}{$\frac{390}{78}+\frac{460}{92}$}\right)$\\
p_{$\text{total }$$}=36 $\mathrm{ mm}$
\end{gathered}$
Mole fraction of toluene in vapour phase \(\left(Y_T\right)\) can be calculated as below :
\(p_T^{{}^{\circ}} \chi_T=Y_T, p_{\text{total }} \Rightarrow Y_T=\frac{p_T^{{}^{\circ}} \chi_T}{p_{\text{total }}}\)
where, \(\chi_T\) is mole fraction of toluene.
\(Y_T=\frac{32 \times \frac{1}{2}}{36} \RightarrowY_T=\frac{16}{36}=0.444\)$

Dividing (i) by (ii), we get
$M_y=4 M_x$.

6672.text: If the middle term in the expansion of $(1+x)^{2 n}$ is the greatest term, then $x$ lies in the interval
6672.sol:
In the expansion of $(1+x)^{2 n}$, middle term is ${ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n x^n$. Since, middle term is the greatest term.
$\therefore{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n x^n > { }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n-1} x^{n-1}\text{ and }{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_r x^n > { }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1} x^{n+1}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad x > \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n-1}}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n} \text{ and } x < \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}} \\
& \text{ Hence, } x \in\left(\frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}, \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}\right)
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $x \in\left(\frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}, \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}\right)\begin{aligned}
& x \in\left($\begin{array}{c}
$\frac{(2 n) !}{(n-1) !(2 n-n+1)}$ \times $\frac{n !(2 n-n) !}{(2 n) !}$ \\
$\frac{(2 n) !}{n !(2 n-n) !}$ \times $\frac{(n-1) !(2 n-n+1)}{(2 n) !}$
\end{array}$\right) \\
& x \in\left(\frac{n(n-1) ! n !}{n(n-1) !(n+1) n !}, \frac{(n+1) n !(n-1) !}{n(n-1) ! n !}\right) \\
& \therefore \quad x \in\left(\frac{n}{n+1}, \frac{n+1}{n}\right)
\end{aligned}$

7421.subject: Mathematics
7421.text: If \(\omega\) represents a complex cube root of unity, then \(\left(1+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(1+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)+\left(2+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(2+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)\) \(+\ldots+\left(n+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(n+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)=\)
7421.sol:
As \(\omega\) is complex cube root of unity, then
\(\begin{aligned}
& 1+\omega+\omega^2=0 \text{ and } \omega^3=1 \quad \ldots (i) \\
& \because\left(r+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(r+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)=r^2+r\left(\frac{1}{\omega}+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right)+\frac{1}{\omega^3} \\
& =r^2+\left(\frac{\omega^2+\omega}{\omega^3}\right) r+\frac{1}{\omega^3}=r^2-r+1 \quad \text{ [from Eq. (i)] } \\
& \text{ Now, } \sum_{r=1}^n\left(r+\frac{1}{\omega}\right)\left(r+\frac{1}{\omega^2}\right) \\
& =\sum_{r=1}^n\left(r^2-r+1\right)=\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}-\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+n \\
& =\frac{n(n+1)}{6}[2 n+1-3]+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{6}(2 n-2)+n \\
& =\frac{n}{3}\left(n^2-1\right)+n=\frac{n}{3}\left[n^2-1+3\right]=\frac{n\left(n^2+2\right)}{3}
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (2) is correct.

The point $(\lambda, \lambda-2)$ lies inside the ellipse $\begin{aligned} \text{ and } 4 x²+9 y²=36 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \quad 4 \lambda^2+9(\lambda-2)^2 < 36 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \quad 4 \lambda^2+9 \lambda^2+36-36 \lambda < 36 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \quad 13 \lambda^2-36 \lambda < 0 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \lambda(13 \lambda-36) < 0 \\ \text{ and } \Rightarrow \quad 0 < \lambda < \frac{36}{13}
\end{aligned} The point $(\lambda, \lambda-2)$ also lies outside the parabola $y^2=x
$\begin{aligned}$& (\lambda-2)^2-\lambda>0 \\
\Rightarrow & \lambda^2-4 \lambda+4-\lambda>0 \Rightarrow \lambda^2-5 \lambda+4>0 \\
\Rightarrow & \lambda^2-4 \lambda-\lambda+4>0 \Rightarrow(\lambda-4)(\lambda-1)>0 \\
\Rightarrow & \lambda \in(-$\infty,1) \cup(4, $\infty)
\end{aligned} From $Eqs. (i) and (ii), we can conclude that 0 < \lambda < 1$

Eccentricity,

So, the focus will be
$\left( \pm \frac{12}{5} \times \frac{15}{12}, 0\right) \text{ i.e., }( \pm 3,0)$
On comparing the focus of ellipse with hyperbola, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt{16-b^2}=3 \\
& 16-b^2=9 \\
& b^2=7

14344.text: In an oscillating \(L C\) circuit, the maximum charge on the capacitor is \(Q\). The charge on the capacitor when the energy is stored equally between the electric and magnetic fields is
14344.sol:
Given, in an oscillating \(L C\) circuit, maximum charge on the capacitor \(=Q\) We know that, total energy stored in the capacitor,
\$U=\frac{1}{2} \frac{Q^2}{C}$\(\therefore\) Energy is equally distributed$ in $a electric field and magnetic field, so the energy stored in the capacitor is half of maximum.
\(\therefore \frac{1}{2}\) (energy stored in \(C\), in electric field) \(=\) energy stored in \(C\), in magnetic field
\($\begin{array}{rlrl} \therefore & \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} \frac{Q^2}{C} =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{Q^{\prime 2}}{C}\\
\text{ or }& \frac{1}{4} \frac{Q^2}{C} =\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{Q^{\prime 2}}{C}\\
\text{ or }& Q^{\prime 2} =\frac{2 Q^2}{4}\\
\text{ or }& Q^{\prime} =\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}
\end{array}$
Hence, the charge on the capacitor when the energy is started equally between the electric and magnetic field is $\frac{Q}{\sqrt{2}}$.$

15121.text:
Two infinitely long wires each carrying the same current and pointing in $+ y$ direction are placed in the $xy$- plane, at $x = - 2cm$ and $x = 1cm$. An electron is fired with speed $U$ from the origin making an angle of $+ 45 °$ from the $x$ - axis. The force on the electron at the instant it is fired is
[ ${B}_{0}$ is the magnitude of the field at origin due to the wire at $x = 1cm$ alone].
15121.sol:
Magnetic field at origin due to wire at $x = 1cm$ is

${B}_{0} = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}i}{2\pi\left(0 . 01\right)} ⊙$

Magnetic field at origin due to wire at $x = - 2cm$ is

$B = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}i}{2\pi\left(0 . 02\right)} ⊗$

Therefore, the net magnetic field at origin will be,

$\overset{\to}{B}net = \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}i}{2\pi\left(0 . 02\right)} ⊙ = \dfrac{{B}_{0}}{2}\overset{^}{k}$

The velocity of the electron is given as $\overset{\to}{v} = \dfrac{U}{\sqrt{2}}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{U}{\sqrt{2}}\overset{^}{j}$

The force on the electron will be,

$\overset{\to}{F} = e\overset{\to}{v} \times \overset{\to}{B} = e\left(\dfrac{U}{\sqrt{2}}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{U}{\sqrt{2}}\overset{^}{j}\right) \times \dfrac{{B}_{0}}{2}\overset{^}{k} ⇒ \overset{\to}{F} = \dfrac{- eU{B}_{0}}{2\sqrt{2}}\left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j}\right)$

18625.subject: Mathematics
18625.text: The variance of 20 observations is 5. If each observation is multiplied by 2 , then the new variance of the resulting observation is
18625.sol:
Let the observations be $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{20}$ and $\bar{x}$ be their mean. Given that, variance $=5$ and $n= 20. We know that,
Variance \left(\sigma^2\right)=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{20}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2$
i.e. $5=\frac{1}{20} \sum_{i=1}^{20}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2$
or $\sum_{i=1}^{20}\left(x_i-\bar{x}\right)^2=100$ .....(i)
If each observation is multiplied by 2 and the new resulting observations are $y_i$, then
$y_i=2 x_i$ i.e., $x_i=\frac{1}{2} y_i$
Therefore,
$\overline{\mathrm{y}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{n}} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{20} \mathrm{y}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{1}{20} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{20} 2 \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}=2 \cdot \frac{1}{20} \sum_{\mathrm{i}=1}^{20} \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}$
i.e., $\bar{y}=2 \bar{x}$ or $\bar{x}=\frac{1}{2} \bar{y}$.
On substituting the values of $x_i$ and $\bar{x}$ in eq. (i), we get
$\sum_{i=1}^{20}\left(\frac{1}{2} y_i-\frac{1}{2} \bar{y}\right)^2=100$
i.e., $\sum_{i=1}^{20}\left(y_i-\bar{y}\right)^2=400$
Thus, the variance of new observations
$=\frac{1}{20} \times 400=20=2^2 \times 5$.

19595.subject: Chemistry
19595.text:
A Nitrogen containing organic compound with molecular formula C$_3$H$_5$N undergoes the following reactions.
C$_3$H$_5$N + Na / Hg in C$_2$H$_5$OH $\rightarrow$ [A]
[A] + CH$_3$COCl / NaOH (aq) $\rightarrow$ [B]
[A] + CHCl$_3$ / KOH on heating $\rightarrow$ [C] (foul smelling compound)
Identify compounds [B] and [C]
19595.sol:
The molecular formula of the given organic compound is $C_3H_5N$. Its degree of unsaturation is $3 + 1 - \dfrac{5}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} = 2$.

The compound undergoes reduction to form [A], which reacts with $CHC$l_3$ and KOH to give a foul-smelling compound [C]. This is the carbylamine reaction, which is characteristic of primary amines. Thus, [A] is a primary amine.

Since [A] is a primary amine obtained by the reduction of a compound with degree of unsaturation 2, the original compound $C_3H_5N$ must be an alkyl cyanide (nitrile). Therefore, $C_3H_5N$ is propanenitrile, $CH_3-CH_2-CN$.

Reduction of propanenitrile with Na/Hg in $C_2H_5OH$ yields propan-1-amine:
$CH_3-CH_2-CN \xrightarrow{Na/Hg, C_2H_5OH} CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2$ ([A])

Reaction of propan-1-amine [A] with acetyl chloride ($CH_3COCl$) in the presence of NaOH (aq) results in acetylation to form N-propylacetamide:
$CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{NaOH} CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH-COCH_3 + HCl$
Thus, [B] is $CH_3-(CH_2)_2-NH-COCH_3$.

Reaction of propan-1-amine [A] with $CHCl_3$ and KOH on heating yields propyl isocyanide, which is the foul-smelling compound:
$CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2 + CHCl_3 + 3KOH \xrightarrow{$\Delta$} CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-NC + 3KCl + 3H_2O$
Thus, [C] is $CH_3-(CH_2)_2-NC$.

Answer: [B]: CH_3-$(CH_2$)_2-$NH$-$COCH_3$ [C]: CH_3-$(CH_2$)_2-$NC

20644.subject: Chemistry
20644.text: When $9.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{ kg}$ of formic acid is added to 600 ml of water the freezing point of water is depressed. If $30 \%$ of Formic acid undergoes dissociation what would be the freezing point of the solution? ( $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}$ of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is $1.86 \mathrm{ K} \mathrm{ kg} \mathrm{ mol} ; \mathrm{MM}$ of formic acid: 46 amu )
20644.sol:
The molar mass of formic acid (HCOOH) is $46 \text{ g/mol}$. The mass of formic acid is $9.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} = 9.2 \text{ g}$.

The number of moles of formic acid is $n = \dfrac{9.2}{46} = 0.2 \text{ mol}$.

The mass of water is $600 \text{ ml} = 0.6 \text{ kg}$. The molality $m$ is $\dfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ mol/kg}$.

Formic acid dissociates as $\text{HCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \textH^{+} + \text{HCOO}^{-}$. For $30\%$ dissociation, the degree of dissociation $\alpha = 0.3$.

The van't Hoff factor $i = 1 + \alpha(n-1)$, where $n=2$. Thus, $i = 1 + 0.3(2-1) = 1.3$.

The depression in freezing point is $\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m = 1.3 \times 1.86 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1.3 \times 0.62 = 0.806 \text{ K}$.

The freezing point of the solution is $T_f = T_f^{{}^{\circ}} - \Delta T_f = 273.15 - 0.806 = 272.344 \text{ K}$.

Answer: 272.3 K

21088.text: The coefficient of $x^{29}$ in the expansion of $\left(1-3 x+3 x^2-x^3\right)^{15}$ is
21088.sol:
The given expression is $\left(1 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3\right)^{15}$.

Observe that $1 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3 = (1 - x)^3$.

Substituting this into the expression, we get $((1 - x)^3)^{15} = (1 - x)^{45}$.

The general term in the binomial expansion of $(1 - x)^{n}$ is given by $^{n}C_{r} (1)^{n-r} (-x)^{r} = ^{n}C_{r} (-1)^{r} x^{r}$.

For the expansion of $(1 - x)^{45}$, the term containing $x^{29}$ corresponds to $r = 29$.

The coefficient is $^{45}C_{29} (-1)^{29} = -^{45}C_{29}$.

Since $^{45}C_{29} = ^{45}C_{45-29} = ^{45}C_{16}$, the coefficient is $-^{45}C_{16}$.

Answer: $-\binom{45}{16}$

21252.subject: Mathematics
21252.text: $\text{ The value of the integral } \int_\limits{\dfrac{1}{3}}^1 \dfrac{\left(x-x^3\right)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} d x \text{$ is }
21252.sol:
Let $I = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x-x^3)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx$.

Factor out $x^3$ from the term inside the cube root:

$I = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x^3(x^{-2}-1))^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{x(x^{-2}-1)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^4} dx = \int_{\dfrac{1}{3}}^{1} \dfrac{(x^{-2}-1)^{\dfrac{1}{3}}}{x^3} dx$.

Let $u = x^{-2} - 1$. Then $du = -2x^{-3} dx$, which implies $x^{-3} dx = -\dfrac{1}{2} du$.

Change the limits of integration:

When $x = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $u = (\dfrac{1}{3})^{-2} - 1 = 9 - 1 = 8$.

When $x = 1$, $u = 1^{-2} - 1 = 0$.

Substituting these into the integral:

$I = \int_{8}^{0} u^{\dfrac{1}{3}} (-\dfrac{1}{2}) du = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{8} u^{\dfrac{1}{3}} du$.

Evaluating the integral:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} [\dfrac{u^{\dfrac{4}{3}}}{\dfrac{4}{3}}]_{0}^{8} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{3}{4} [u^{\dfrac{4}{3}}]_{0}^{8} = \dfrac{3}{8} (8^{\dfrac{4}{3}} - 0) = \dfrac{3}{8} \times (2^3)^{\dfrac{4}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 2^4 = \dfrac{3}{8} \times 16 = 3 \times 2 = 6$.

Answer: 6

21491.text: If the distance between the foci and the distance between the two directrixes are in the ratio $3: 2$ for a hyperbola $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$, then a : b is

$b^2 = a^2 \left( \dfrac{3}{2} -1 \right) = a^2 \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)

\dfrac{b^2}{a^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}

\dfrac{b}{a} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}

Therefore, \dfrac{a}{b} = \sqrt{2}$: 1$.

Answer: \sqrt{2}$: 1

22038.text:
Set $P=\{x: x$ is a multiple of 4 less than 40$\}Q=\{x: x$ is an odd multiple of 7 less than 50$\}R=\{x: x$ is a multiple of 6 less than 50$\}$
Then $n(P \cup Q \cup R)=$
22038.sol:
The set $P$ consists of multiples of 4 less than 40. $P = \{4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36\}$. Thus, $n(P) = 9$.

The set $Q$ consists of odd multiples of 7 less than 50. $Q = \{7, 21, 35, 49\}$. Thus, $n(Q) = 4$.

The set $R$ consists of multiples of 6 less than 50. $R = \{6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48\}$. Thus, $n(R) = 8$.

We find the intersections:
$P \cap Q = \emptyset$ (no odd multiple of 7 is a multiple of 4).
$P \cap R = \{12, 24, 36\}$, so $n(P \cap R) = 3$.
$Q \cap R = \emptyset$ (no odd multiple of 7 is a multiple of 6).
$P \cap Q \cap R = \emptyset$.

Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion:
$n(P \cup Q \cup R) = n(P) + n(Q) + n(R) - n(P \cap Q) - n(P \cap R) - n(Q \cap R) + n(P \cap Q \cap R)$
$n(P \cup Q \cup R) = 9 + 4 + 8 - 0 - 3 - 0 + 0 = 18$.

Answer: 18

22198.text: The coordinates of the vertices of the triangle are $A(-2,3,6), B(-4,4,9)$ and $C(0,5,8)$. The direction cosines of the median $\mathrm{BE}$ are
22198.sol:
The median BE connects vertex B to the midpoint E of side AC. The coordinates of A are $(-2, 3, 6)$ and C are $(0, 5, 8)$.

The midpoint E of AC is given by $E = \left( \dfrac{-2 + 0}{2}, \dfrac{3 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{6 + 8}{2} \right) = (-1, 4, 7)$.

The vector $\overrightarrow{BE}$ is given by $E - B = (-1 - (-4), 4 - 4, 7 - 9) = (3, 0, -2)$.

The magnitude of vector $\overrightarrow{BE}$ is $|\overrightarrow{BE}| = \sqrt{3^2 + 0^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 0 + 4} = \sqrt{13}$.

The direction cosines of the vector $\overrightarrow{BE}$ are obtained by dividing the components of the vector by its magnitude:

$\left( \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}, \dfrac{0}{\sqrt{13}}, \dfrac{-2}{\sqrt{13}} \right) = \left( \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}, 0, -\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \right)$.

Answer: $\left\langle\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}, \quad 0, \quad-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\right\rangle$

22941.subject: Physics
22941.text: What is the ratio of the mean free paths of the molecules of two gases $A$ and $B$ having the molecular diameters $2 \mathrm{ A}^0$ and $3 \mathrm{ A}^0$ respectively under the identical conditions of pressure, temperature and volume?
22941.sol:
The mean free path $\lambda$ of a gas molecule is given by the formula $\lambda = \dfrac{k_B T}{\sqrt{2} \pi d^2 P}$, where $k_B$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ is the temperature, $d$ is the molecular diameter, and $P$ is the pressure.

Under identical conditions of pressure, temperature, and volume, the variables $k_B$, $T$, and $P$ are constant for both gases $A$ and $B$.

Therefore, the mean free path is inversely proportional to the square of the molecular diameter: $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{d^2}$.

Given the diameters $d_A = 2 \text{ \AA}$ and $d_B = 3 \text{ \AA}$, the ratio of the mean free paths is:

$\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = \dfrac{d_B^2}{d_A^2} = \left( \dfrac{3}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B} = 9:4$.

Answer: $\dfrac{\lambda_A}{\lambda_B}=9: 4$

23601.text: The dimensional formula for specific resistance is:
23601.sol:
Specific resistance $\rho$ is given by $\rho = \dfrac{R A}{L}$.

Resistance $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{W}{q I} = \dfrac{W}{I^2 t}$.

Dimensional formula of work $W = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$.

Dimensional formula of current $I = [A]$ and time $t = [T]$.

Dimensional formula of resistance $R = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[A^2 T]} = [M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$.

Dimensional formula of area $A = [L^2]$ and length $L = [L]$.

Dimensional formula of specific resistance $\rho = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-3} A^{-2}] [L^2]}{[L]} = [M L^3 T^{-3} A^{-2}]$.

Answer: $[M\,L^3\,T^{-3}\,A^{-2}]$

26146.text:
A rectangular conducting loop of length $4cm$ and width $2cm$ is in the $xy$-plane, as shown in the figure. It is being moved away from a thin and long conducting wire along the direction $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\overset{∧}{x} + \dfrac{1}{2}\overset{∧}{y}$ with a constant speed $v$. The wire is carrying a steady current $I = 10A$ in the positive $x$-direction. A current of $10\muA$ flows through the loop when it is at a distance $d = 4cm$ from the wire. If the resistance of the loop is $0 . 1Ω$, then the value of $v$ is _____ $m{s}^{- 1}$.

[Given: The permeability of free space ${\mu}_{0} = 4\pi \times {10}^{- 7}N{A}^{- 2}$]
26146.sol:
The two sides of the rectangular loop which are perpendicular to the wire would not contribute in induced emf.

Angle of velocity vector with x-axis is $tan\alpha = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. Therefore, $\alpha = 30 °$.

For parallel sides:

$\overset{\to}{E} = \overset{\to}{B} \times \overset{\to}{v}$

$= \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}I}{2\pix} \times v$

$⇒$ Net emf $= \left({E}_{1}cos{60}^{o} - {E}_{2}cos{60}^{o}\right) \times$width

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{2}{100} \times \dfrac{{\mu}_{0}Iv}{2\pi}\left[\dfrac{1}{\dfrac{4}{100}} - \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{8}{100}}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{100} \times \left(2 \times {10}^{- 7}\right) \times 10 \times v \times \dfrac{100}{8}$

$= 2 . 5v \times {10}^{- 7}$

Now, net EMF $= i \times R$

$⇒ v = \dfrac{\left(10 \times {10}^{- 6}\right) \times 0 . 1}{2 . 5 \times {10}^{- 7}} = 4m{s}^{- 1}$

26190.subject: Physics
26190.text:
In the figure, the inner (shaded) region $A$ represents a sphere of radius ${r}_{A} = 1$, within which the electrostatic charge density varies with the radial distance $r$ from the center as ${ρ}_{A} = kr$, where $k$ is positive. In the spherical shell $B$ of outer radius ${r}_{B}$, the electrostatic charge density varies as ${ρ}_{B} = \dfrac{2k}{r}$. Assume that dimensions are taken care of. All physical quantities are in their SI units.

​​​​​​​

Which of the following statement(s) is/(are) correct?
options: If ${r}_{B} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3}{2}}$, then the electric field is zero everywhere outside $B$.
If ${r}_{B} = \dfrac{3}{2}$, then the electric potential just outside $B$ is $\dfrac{k}{{ε}_{0}}$.
If ${r}_{B} = 2$, then the total charge of the configuration is $15\pik .$
If ${r}_{B} = \dfrac{5}{2}$, then the magnitude of the electric field just outside $B$ is $\dfrac{13\pik}{{ε}_{0}}$.
26190.sol:
Since both the densities are positive, the total charge can not be zero. Hence, option A is incorrect.

For total charge,

${Q}_{Total} = {∫}_{0}^{{r}_{A}}kr\left(4\pi{r}^{2}\right)dr + {∫}_{{r}_{A}}^{{r}_{B}}\dfrac{2k}{r}\left(4\pi{r}^{2}\right)dr$

$= \dfrac{4\pik}{4}{r}_{A}^{4} + \dfrac{8\pik}{2}\left({r}_{B}^{2} - {r}_{A}^{2}\right)$

$= \pik + 4\pik\left({r}_{B}^{2} - {r}_{A}^{2}\right)$

If ${r}_{B} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

${Q}_{Total} = \pik + 4\pik\left(\dfrac{9}{4} - 1\right)$

$= \pik + 4\pik\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right) = 6\pik$

The potential just outside $B$ will be,

$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{{Q}_{total}}{{r}_{B}} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{6\pik}{{r}_{B}} = \dfrac{3k}{2}\dfrac{2}{3{ε}_{0}} = \dfrac{k}{{ε}_{0}}$

Hence, option B is correct.

If ${r}_{B} = 2$

${Q}_{Total} = \pik + 4\pik\left(4 - 1\right)$$= 13\pik$

Hence, option C is incorrect

If ${r}_{B} = \dfrac{5}{2}$

${Q}_{Total} = \pik + 4\pik\left(\dfrac{25}{4} - 1\right)$

$= \pik + \pik\left(21\right)$

$= 22\pik$

Therefore, the electric field just outside B will be,

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{{Q}_{Total}}{{{r}_{B}}^{2}}\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{22\pik}{25} \times 4$$= \dfrac{22k}{25{ε}_{0}}$

Hence, option D is incorrect.

26511.subject: Physics
26511.text: A beam of polychromatic light passes through a thin prism of prism angle $6^\circ$. The refractive index of the material of the prism varies with wavelength $(\lambda)$ as $n(\lambda) = \alpha\lambda + \dfrac{\beta}{\lambda^2}$, where $\alpha = 3\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$ and $\beta = 0.096\ \mu\text{m}^2$. If $\lambda_{\min}$ is the wavelength at which the angle of minimum deviation $D_m$ is smallest, then the correct value of $D_m$ at $\lambda_{\min}$ is
26511.sol:
For a thin prism, the angle of deviation is given by $D = (n - 1)A$.

To find the smallest value of deviation $D_m$, we need to find the minimum value of the refractive index $n(\lambda)$.

Given $n(\lambda) = \alpha\lambda + \dfrac{\beta}{\lambda^2}$.

Differentiating $n(\lambda)$ with respect to $\lambda$ and equating to zero for minimum:

$\dfrac{dn}{d\lambda} = \alpha - \dfrac{2\beta}{\lambda^3} = 0$

$\lambda^3 = \dfrac{2\beta}{\alpha}$

Substituting the given values $\alpha = 3\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$ and $\beta = 0.096\ \mu\text{m}^2$:

$\lambda^3 = \dfrac{2 \times 0.096}{3} = 0.064$

$\lambda = 0.4\ \mu\text{m}$

Now, substituting $\lambda = 0.4\ \mu\text{m}$ back into the expression for $n(\lambda)$:

$n_{\min} = 3(0.4) + \dfrac{0.096}{(0.4)^2}$

$n_{\min} = 1.2 + \dfrac{0.096}{0.16} = 1.2 + 0.6 = 1.8$

The smallest angle of deviation is:

$D_m = (n_{\min} - 1)A$

$D_m = (1.8 - 1) \times 6^\circ = 0.8 \times 6^\circ = 4.8^\circ$

Answer: $4.8^\circ$

27017.subject: Chemistry
27017.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement-I: The condensation reaction between $CH_3-CH=O$ and under optimum pH will produce .

Statement-II: The molecule will generate $Ph-CH=O$ in the presence of dilute acid.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
27017.sol:
In Statement-I, evaluating the structure of semicarbazide ($\text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{NH}_2$), the lone pair of electrons on the $-\text{NH}_2$ group directly attached to the carbonyl carbon is delocalized due to resonance. The terminal $-\text{NH}_2$ group of the hydrazine part is not involved in resonance with the carbonyl group, making it significantly more nucleophilic.

Therefore, the condensation reaction of acetaldehyde with semicarbazide under optimum pH occurs at the terminal $-\text{NH}_2$ group to yield acetaldehyde semicarbazone:

$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

The product provided in Statement-I indicates an attack by the less nucleophilic amide nitrogen to form $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{N}-\text{C}(=\text{O})-\text{NH}-\text{NH}_2$, which is incorrect. Thus, Statement-I is false.

In Statement-II, the given molecule $\text{Ph}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})(\text{OCH}_3)$ is a hemiacetal. Hemiacetals are unstable in the presence of dilute aqueous acid and undergo rapid hydrolysis to regenerate the corresponding carbonyl compound and alcohol.

$\text{Ph}-\text{CH}(\text{OH})(\text{OCH}_3) \xrightarrow{\text{dil. H}^+} \text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{O} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}$

This hydrolysis reaction successfully generates benzaldehyde ($\text{Ph}-\text{CH}=\text{O}$). Thus, Statement-II is true.

We conclude that Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true.

27020.subject: Chemistry
27020.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Cross aldol condensation between two different aldehydes will always produce four different products.
Statement II: When semicarbazide reacts with a mixture of benzaldehyde and acetophenone under optimum pH, it forms a condensation product with acetophenone only.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
27020.sol:
Statement I: Cross aldol condensation between two different aldehydes produces four products only if both aldehydes have $\alpha$-hydrogen atoms. If one aldehyde lacks $\alpha$-hydrogen (e.g., benzaldehyde and acetaldehyde), only two products are typically formed (one self and one cross). If neither has $\alpha$-hydrogen, no aldol condensation occurs. Thus, it does not 'always' produce four products. Statement I is false.

Statement II: Benzaldehyde is an aldehyde and acetophenone is a ketone. Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition reactions due to less steric hindrance and greater electronic deficiency of the carbonyl carbon. Therefore, semicarbazide will react faster with benzaldehyde than with acetophenone. The statement claiming it forms a product with acetophenone only is incorrect. Statement II is false.

28530.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
28530.text: For elements $B, C, NLi, Be, OandF$, the correct order of first ionisation enthalpy is
options: $Li < Be < B < C < O < N < F$
$B < Li < Be < C < N < O < F$
$Li < Be < B < C < N < O < F$
$Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F$
28530.sol:
The first ionisation energy varies predictably across the periodic table. As we move from left to right across a period, the ionisation energy of elements increases. This is due to the decrease in the size of atoms across a period. The valence electrons get closer to the nucleus of an atom as we move from left to right due to increased nuclear charge. The force of attraction between the nucleus and the electrons increases and hence more energy is required to remove an electron from the valence shell. Ionisation energy of boron being unexpectedly less than that for beryllium due to the 2s orbital being totally filled in beryllium, whereas boron has one electron in a 2p orbital as well, and the 2s orbital is shielded much more than the 2p orbital. Ionisation energy is more for nitrogen than oxygen because nitrogen is more stable due to its half-filled electronic configuration.

$Li < B < Be < C < O < N < F$

31929.text: If $5$ moles of ${BaCl}_{2}$ is mixed with $2$ moles of ${Na}_{3}{PO}_{4},$ the maximum number of moles of ${Ba}_{3}{\left({PO}_{4}\right)}_{2}$formed is $_________$ (Nearest integer)

The balanced chemical equation for the reaction between ${BaCl}_{2}$ and ${Na}_{3}{PO}_{4}$ is:

$3{BaCl}_{2} + 2{Na}_{3}{PO}_{4} \to {Ba}_{3} ( {PO}_{4}{)}_{2} + 6NaCl$

$5$ moles of barium chloride will require $\dfrac{5 \times 2}{3} = 3 . 3$ moles of sodium phosphate.

Here, sodium phosphate is the limiting reagent.
$2$ moles of sodium phosphate produce $1$ mole of barium phosphate.

Thus,$2$ moles of sodium phosphate will produce$1$ mole of barium phosphate.

Hence, the maximum no. of moles of ${Ba}_{3} ( {PO}_{4}{)}_{2}$that can be formed is one mole.

Clearly it is always negative in $[ 0, 1 ]$

minimum value would be at $x = 1$.

$\dfrac{{( 1 + 1 )}^{0.6}}{1 + {\left(1\right)}^{0.6}} = \dfrac{{2}^{0.6}}{2} = {2}^{- 0.4} = k$

35850.subject: Mathematics
35850.sol:
$~ \left(p ⇔ ~ q\right) ∧ q$ $= \left(p ⇔ q\right) ∧ q$

Proof: Solving the given $~ \left(p ⇔ ~ q\right)$

$= ~ \left(\left(p \to ~ q\right) ∧ \left(~ q \to p\right)\right)$

$= ~ \left(\left(~ p ∨ ~ q\right) ∧ \left(q ∨ p\right)\right)$

$= ~ \left(~ \left(p ∧ q\right) ∧ \left(p ∨ q\right)\right)$

$= \left(p ∧ q\right) ∨ ~ \left(p ∨ q\right) . . . \left(1\right)$

Now, $p ⇔ q ≡ \left(p \to q\right) ∧ \left(q \to p\right)$

$= \left(~ p ∨ q\right) ∧ \left(~ q ∨ p\right)$

$= \left(~ p ∨ q\right) ∧ ~ q ∨ \left(~ p ∨ q\right) ∧ p$

$= \left(~ p ∧ ~ q\right) ∨ \left(q ∧ ~ q\right) ∨ \left(\left(~ p ∧ p\right) ∨ \left(q ∧ p\right)\right)$

$= \left(~ p ∧ ~ q\right) ∨ c ∨ \left(c ∨ \left(q ∧ p\right)\right)$ $\left\{\text{where c is contradiction}\right\}$

$= ~ p ∧ ~ q ∨ \left(p ∧ q\right)$

$= ~ \left(p ∨ q\right) ∨ \left(p ∧ q\right) . . . \left(2\right)$

So from equation $\left(1\right) \text{ and } \left(2\right)$ we get

$~ \left(p ⇔ ~ q\right) ∧ q ≡ \left(p ⇔ q\right) ∧ q$

$p$ $q$ $p ↔ q$ $\left(p ↔ q\right) ∧ q$ $\left(p \to q\right)$ $\left(p \to q\right) ∧ q$ $\left(p \to 1\right) ∧ p$
$T$ $T$ $T$ $T$ $T$ $T$ $T$
$T$ $F$ $F$ $F$ $F$ $F$ $F$
$F$ $T$ $F$ $F$ $T$ $T$ $F$
$F$ $F$ $T$ $F$ $T$ $F$ $F$

$∴ \left(~ \left(p ⇔ ~ q\right)\right) ∧ q$ is equivalent to $\left(p ⇒ q\right) ∧ p$.

36167.subject: Mathematics
36167.text: Let $\mathbf{A}$ be a square matrix all of whose entries are integers. Then which one of the following is true?
options:
If $\operatorname{det} A=\pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ exists but all its entries are not necessarily integers

If $\operatorname{det} A \neq \pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ exists and all its entries are non-integers

If $\operatorname{det} A=\pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ exists and all its entries are integers

If $\operatorname{det} A=\pm 1$, then $A^{-1}$ need not exist
36167.sol:
Each entry of $A$ is integer, so the cofactor of every entry is an integer and hence each entry in the adjoint of matrix $A$ is integer.
Now $\operatorname{det} A=\pm 1$ and $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{det}(A)}(\operatorname{adj} A)$
$\Rightarrow$ all entries in $\mathrm{A}^{-1}$ are integers.

36594.text: Three rotten apples are accidently mixed with fifteen good apples. Assuming the random variable $x$ to be the number of rotten apples in a draw of two apples, the variance of $x$ is
36594.sol:
Given apples are: $3$ bad, $15$ good

Let $X$ be no. of bad apples.

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{{}^{15}{C}_{2}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{15 !}{2 ! \times 13 !}}{\dfrac{18 !}{2 ! \times 16 !}}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{15 \times 14}{18 \times 17} = \dfrac{5 \times 7}{3 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 0\right) = \dfrac{35}{51}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 1\right) = \dfrac{{}^{3}{C}_{1}{\times}^{15}{C}_{1}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{3 \times 15}{9 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 1\right) = \dfrac{5}{17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 2\right) = \dfrac{{}^{3}{C}_{2}}{{}^{18}{C}_{2}} = \dfrac{3}{9 \times 17}$

$⇒ P\left(X = 2\right) = \dfrac{3}{153}$

$⇒ E\left(X\right) = 0 \times \dfrac{35}{51} + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{17} + 2 \times \dfrac{3}{153}$

$⇒ E\left(X\right) = \dfrac{1}{3}$

We know that, $Var\left(X\right) = E\left({X}^{2}\right) - {\left(E\left(X\right)\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = 0 \times \dfrac{35}{51} + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{17} + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{51} - {\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = \dfrac{19}{51} - \dfrac{1}{9}$

$⇒ Var\left(X\right) = \dfrac{40}{153}$

36821.subject: Mathematics
36821.text: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 - 3x + r = 0$, and $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}, 2\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 + 3x + r = 0$. If the roots of the equation $x^2 + 6x = m$ are $2\alpha + \beta + 2r$ and $\alpha - 2\beta - \dfrac{r}{2}$, then $m$ is equal to:
36821.sol:
From the first equation $x^2 - 3x + r = 0$, the sum and product of the roots are:

$\alpha + \beta = 3$

$\alpha \beta = r$

From the second equation $x^2 + 3x + r = 0$, the sum and product of the roots are:

$\dfrac{\alpha}{2} + 2\beta = -3$

$\left(\dfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)(2\beta) = r \Rightarrow \alpha \beta = r$

We have a system of linear equations in terms of $\alpha and \beta$:

$\alpha + \beta = 3$

$\alpha + 4\beta = -6$

Subtracting the first equation from the second gives:

$3\beta = -9 \Rightarrow \beta = -3$

Substituting $\beta = -3$ into $\alpha + \beta = 3$ gives:

$\alpha = 6$

Now, we can find $r$:

$r = \alpha \beta = 6 \times (-3) = -18$

The roots of the third equation $x^2 + 6x - m = 0$ are given as $2\alpha + \beta + 2r$ and $\alpha - 2\beta - \dfrac{r}{2}$. Let us calculate their values:

$R_1 = 2(6) + (-3) + 2(-18) = 12 - 3 - 36 = -27$

$R_2 = 6 - 2(-3) - \dfrac{-18}{2} = 6 + 6 + 9 = 21$

The product of the roots of the equation $x^2 + 6x - m = 0$ is $-m$. Therefore:

$-m = R_1 R_2 = (-27)(21)$

$-m = -567 \Rightarrow m = 567$

Answer: $567$

37042.text: Let $a_{1}, \frac{a_{2}}{2}, \frac{a_{3}}{2^{2}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{10}}{2^{9}}$ be a G.P. of common ratio $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. If $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{10}=62$, then $a_{1}$ is equal to :
37042.sol:
The G.P. is $a_1, \frac{a_2}{2}, \frac{a_3}{2^2}, \ldots, \frac{a_{10}}{2^9}$ with common ratio $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$.
So $\frac{a_n}{2^{n-1}} = a_1 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^{n-1}$, giving $a_n = a_1 \cdot (\sqrt{2})^{n-1}$.
$\sum_{n=1}^{10} a_n = a_1 \cdot \frac{(\sqrt{2})^{10} - 1}{\sqrt{2} - 1} = a_1 \cdot \frac{31}{\sqrt{2} - 1} = 31a_1(\sqrt{2} + 1)$.
Setting this equal to 62: $a_1 = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}+1} = 2(\sqrt{2}-1)$.

$⇒ {a}_{p} = a{\left[\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\dfrac{1}{4}\right]}^{p - 1} . . . \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ a{\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)}^{5} = a\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)\dfrac{p - 1}{4}$

$⇒ 5 = \dfrac{p - 1}{4}$

37579.text: The mean of $6$ distinct observations is $6 . 5$ and their variance is $10 . 25 .$ If $4$ out of $6$ observations are $2, 4, 5$ and $7,$ then the remaining two observations are:
37579.sol:
Let the other two observations be $a and b$, then

$\dfrac{a + b + 2 + 4 + 5 + 7}{6} = 6 . 5$

$⇒ a + b = 21$

$⇒ b = 21 - a$

Then, other two numbers are a and $\left(21 - a\right)$

Now, variance is $10 . 25$, therefore

$10 . 25 = \dfrac{\left(4 + 16 + 25 + 49 + {a}^{2} + {\left(21 - a\right)}^{2}\right)}{6} - {\left(6 . 5\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ 6\left(10 . 25\right) + 6{\left(6 . 5\right)}^{2} = 94 + {a}^{2} + {\left(21 - a\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ {a}^{2} + {\left(21 - a\right)}^{2} = 221$

∴ a = 10 and $\left(21 - a\right) = 21 - 10 = 11$

So, remaining two observations are $10, 11$.

38790.subject: Physics
38790.text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Maximum power is dissipated in a circuit containing an inductor, a capacitor and a resistor connected in series with an $AC$ source, when resonance occurs.

Statement II: Maximum power is dissipated in a circuit containing pure resistor due to zero phase difference between current and voltage.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Statement $I$ is false but Statement $II$ is true
Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are true
Statement $I$ is true but Statement $II$ is false
Both Statement $I$ and Statement $II$ are false
38790.sol:
The formula for impedance is given by

$Z = \sqrt{{R}^{2} + {\left({X}_{L} - {X}_{C}\right)}^{2}}$

At resonance, ${X}_{L} = {X}_{C}$. So, ${Z}_{min} = R$

Power will be maximum when impedance is minimum. Thus the maximum power occurs in a purely resistive circuit.

40433.subject: Physics
40433.text: A thin half ring of radius $35$ cm is uniformly charged with a total charge of $Q$ coulomb. If the magnitude of the electric field at centre of the half ring is $100$ V/m, then the value of $Q$ is _______ nC. ($\epsilon_o = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C$^2$/Nm$^2$ and $\pi = 3.14$)
40433.sol:
The electric field at the center of a uniformly charged half ring is given by:

$E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{R}$

where $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R}$ is the linear charge density.

Substituting $\lambda$, we get:

$E = \dfrac{2kQ}{\pi R^2} = \dfrac{2Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 \pi R^2} = \dfrac{Q}{2\pi^2\epsilon_0 R^2}$

Rearranging for $Q$:

$Q = 2\pi^2\epsilon_0 R^2 E$

Given values:
$E = 100$ V/m
$R = 35$ cm $= 0.35$ m
$\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C$^2$/Nm$^2$
$\pi = 3.14$

Substituting the values:

$Q = 2 \times (3.14)^2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times (0.35)^2 \times 100$

$Q = 2 \times 9.8596 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.1225 \times 100$

$Q \approx 2137.8 \times 10^{-12}$ C

$Q \approx 2.14 \times 10^{-9}$ C $= 2.14$ nC

Answer: $2.14$

40462.subject: Physics
40462.text: An electron is released from rest near an infinite non-conducting sheet of uniform charge density ' $-\sigma$ '. The rate of change of de-Broglie wave length associated with the electron varies inversely as $\mathrm{n}^{\text{th }}$ power of time. The numerical value of $n$ is ________.
40462.sol:
Let the momentum of $\mathrm{e}^{-}$at any time t is p and its de-broglie wavelength is $\lambda$.
Then, $\mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\lambda}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{dp}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{-\mathrm{h}}{\lambda^2} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \mathrm{ma}=\mathrm{F}=-\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\lambda} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}} \quad[\mathrm{~m}=\text{ mass$ of $} \mathrm{e}]
\end{aligned}$
Where, -ve sign represents decrease in $\lambda$ with time
$\mathrm{ma}=\frac{-\mathrm{h}}{(\mathrm{~h} / \mathrm{p})^2} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}}$
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{a}=-\frac{\mathrm{p}^2}{\mathrm{mh}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \mathrm{a}=-\frac{\mathrm{mv}^2}{\mathrm{~h}} \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}} \\ & \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\frac{\mathrm{ah}}{\mathrm{mv}^2}...(1)
\end{aligned}$
here, $\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{qE}}{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{m}} \frac{\sigma}{2 \varepsilon_0}$
$\mathrm{a}=\frac{\sigma \mathrm{e}}{2 \mathrm{~m} \varepsilon_0}$
and $\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{u}+\mathrm{at}$
$\mathrm{v}=\mathrm{at}$
Substituting values of a \& v in equation (1)
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}}=-\frac{2 \mathrm{~h} \varepsilon_0}{\sigma \mathrm{et}^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{~d} \lambda}{\mathrm{dt}} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{t}^2} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{n}=2
\end{aligned}$

41235.sol:
Normal force acting on the coin is, $N = mg$.

Required friction force to provide centripetal force for the coin is, $f = m{\omega}^{2}r$ and maximum value of static friction force available is, $f = \muN = \mumg$.

For limiting condition, we can write

$⇒ \mumg = mr{\omega}^{2}$

$⇒ \omega = \sqrt{\dfrac{\mug}{r}}$

42369.text: An object is projected with kinetic energy $K$ from a point $A$ at an angle $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The ratio of the difference in kinetic energies at points $B$ and $C$ to that at point $A$ (see figure), in the absence of air friction is :
42369.sol:
At A: $KE_A = K$, $v_A = v$, angle $= 60°$.
At B (highest point): $v_B = v\cos 60° = v/2$, so $KE_B = K/4$.
At C (same level as A): by energy conservation, $KE_C = K$.
$|KE_B - KE_C| = |K/4 - K| = 3K/4$.
Ratio $= \frac{3K/4}{K} = \frac{3}{4}$, i.e., $3:4$.

42387.text: A body starts falling freely from height $H$ hits an inclined plane in its path at height $h$. As a result of this perfectly elastic impact, the direction of the velocity of the body becomes horizontal. The value of $\dfrac{H}{h}$ for which the body will take the maximum time to reach the ground is _____.
42387.sol:
Total time of flight $= T$ can be written as, 

$T = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}} + \sqrt{\dfrac{2\left(H - h\right)}{g}}$

For maximum time $= \dfrac{dT}{dh} = 0$

$⇒ \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{g}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{h}} - \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{H - h}}\right) = 0$

$⇒ \sqrt{H - h} = \sqrt{h}$

$⇒ h = \dfrac{H}{2} ⇒ \dfrac{H}{h} = 2$

46711.text: Two coherent light beams of intensities $I$ and $4 I$ are superposed. The maximum and minimum possible intensities in the resulting beam are
46711.sol:
The net intensity due to interference of two beams of intensities \(\mathrm{I}_1, \mathrm{I}_2\) with a phase difference of \(\phi\) is
\(\mathrm{I}_{\text{net }}=\mathrm{I}_1+\mathrm{I}_2+2 \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1} \sqrt{\mathrm{I}_2} \cos \phi\)
Thus, \(\mathrm{I}_{\text{net }_{\text{max }}}\) occurs for \(\cos \phi=1\)
\(\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{\text{net }_{\max }}=\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1}+\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_2}\right)^2=9 \mathrm{I}\)
Similarly, \(\mathrm{I}_{\text{net }_{\min }}\) occurs for \(\cos \phi=-1\)
\(\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}_{\text{net }_{\min }}=\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_1}-\sqrt{\mathrm{I}_2}\right)^2=\mathrm{I}\)

&=\mathrm{x} \log \mathrm{x}-\int \frac{1}{\mathrm{x}} \times \mathrm{x} \mathrm{dx}\\
&=\mathrm{x} \log \mathrm{x}-\int \mathrm{dx}\\

\mathrm{y}&=\mathrm{x}(\log \mathrm{x}-1)+\mathrm{C}\\
\text{ when } \mathrm{x}&=1 \text{ and } \mathrm{y}=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad 0=1(\log 1-1)+\mathrm{C}
\end{aligned}$$
\end{aligned}

 $\begin{array}{ll}

Therefore, angular acceleration \( $=\frac{\omega_{2}-\omega_{1}}{t}=\frac{100 \Pi-60 \Pi}{20}$
\( $=\frac{40 \Pi}{20}=$2 \Pi \)
Thus, angular acceleration$ of $rotating wheel \( =2 \pi$\mathrm{rads}^{-2}$

Let $f\left(x\right) = x^{3} - 14x - 12$

$∵ f\left(4\right) = - 4$

$f\left(4. 1\right) = - 0. 479$

$f\left(4. 2\right) = 3288$

52437.text: A spherical rigid ball is released from rest and starts rolling down an inclined plane from height $h = 7m$, as shown in the figure. It hits a block at rest on the horizontal plane (assume elastic collision). If the mass of both the ball and the block is $m$ and the ball is rolling without sliding, then the speed of the block after collision is close to
52437.sol:
As collision is elastic and masses of colliding objects are equal, so there is exchange of total energy of moving mass to stationary mass.

Hence, velocity of block $=$ velocity of sphere just before collision.

For sphere, if $v =$ velocity of translation of centre of mass at the bottom of plane and $\omega =$ angular speed, then by energy conservation, we have

$mgh = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}I{ω}^{2}$

Here, $\omega = \dfrac{v}{R}$ and $I = \dfrac{2}{5}mR^{2}$

Substituting and solving for velocity, we have

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{7}gh} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10 \times 10 \times 7}{7}} = 10m / s$

$∴$ Velocity of block after collision $= 10m / s$.

54855.subject: Chemistry
54855.text: What is the nature of alcohols in aqueous medium?
54855.sol:
Alcohols are very weak acids, generally weaker than water. In an aqueous medium, they do not ionize to produce $H^+$ or $OH^-$ ions to any appreciable extent.

Because they do not alter the concentration of hydrogen or hydroxyl ions in water, they do not affect the pH of the solution. Consequently, they do not change the colour of red or blue litmus paper.

Therefore, the nature of alcohols in an aqueous medium is neutral.

Answer: Neutral

56666.subject: Chemistry
56666.text: Which form following elements forms coloured compound in its respective oxidation state?
56666.sol:
Transition metal ions form colored compounds when they possess partially filled d-orbitals with unpaired electrons, enabling d-d transitions that absorb visible light.

Analyzing the electronic configurations:

Sc^{3+}$ has configuration $[$\mathrm{Ar}$]\ 3d^0$, Zn^{2+}$ has $[\mathrm{Ar}]\ 3d^{10}$, and Ti^{4+}$ has $[$\mathrm{Ar}$]\ 3d^0$ – all lack the necessary unpaired d-electrons for d-d transitions.

Cr^{3+}$ has configuration $[\mathrm{Ar}]\ 3d^3$ with three unpaired electrons, allowing d-d transitions that produce colored compounds such as the characteristic green or violet chromium(III) compounds.

The ion that forms colored compounds is therefore $\boxed{\mathrm{D}}$.

56768.text: Identify the correct statement from following
options: Lanthanoids have greater tendency to form complexes than actinoids.
Actinoid contraction is greater than lanthanoid contraction.
Hydroxides of actinoids are less basic than Lathanoid hydroxides.
Binding energy of $4 \mathrm{f}$ - orbitals is lower that $5 \mathrm{f}$ - orbitals.
56768.sol:
When a non-volatile solute is added to a solvent, the vapour pressure of the solvent decreases. This is known as the relative lowering of vapour pressure.

Due to the lowering of vapour pressure, the boiling point of the solution increases. This is known as the elevation in boiling point.

Osmotic pressure is a colligative property, meaning it depends on the number of solute particles in the solution. Electrolytes dissociate into ions in solution, resulting in a van't Hoff factor $i > 1$. Non-electrolytes do not dissociate, so $i = 1$. Since osmotic pressure $\pi = iCRT$, an electrolytic solution will have a greater osmotic pressure than a non-electrolytic solution of the same concentration.

The depression in freezing point is a colligative property, not the freezing point itself.

Answer: The osmotic pressure of electrolytic solution is greater than nonelectrolytic solution of the same concentration.

Ozone (

$O_3$

57772.text: Cyclohexene on oxidation by $\text{KMnO}_4$ in dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ produces
57772.sol:
Cyclohexene is a cyclic alkene containing a six-membered ring with one double bond.

When treated with a strong oxidizing agent like $\text{KMnO}_4$ in an acidic medium (dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$), the carbon-carbon double bond undergoes oxidative cleavage.

The ring opens up, and the two vinylic carbon atoms are fully oxidized to carboxylic acid groups.

Since cyclohexene contains six carbon atoms, the resulting product is a straight-chain dicarboxylic acid with six carbon atoms.

The product is $\text{HOOC}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{COOH}$, which is hexane-1,6-dioic acid (commonly known as adipic acid).

Answer: hexane-1,6-dioic acid

59098.text: $40$ gram nonelectrolyte solute having molar mass $180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ dissolved in water has osmotic pressure $2\ \text{atm}$ at $300\ \text{K}$. Calculate the volume of solution. ($\text{R} = 0.0821\ \text{atm mol}^{-1}\textK^{-1}$)
59098.sol:
Using the formula for osmotic pressure:

$\pi = \dfrac{n}{V}RT$

Rearranging for volume $V$:

$V = \dfrac{nRT}{\pi}$

Number of moles of solute $n = \dfrac{40}{180} = \dfrac{2}{9}\ \text{mol}$

Substituting the given values:

$V = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{9} \times 0.0821 \times 300}{2}$

$V = \dfrac{24.63}{9}$

$V = 2.736\ \text{L}$

Since $1\ \text{L} = 1\ \text{dm}^3$, the volume of the solution is $2.74\ \text{dm}^3$.

Answer: $2.74\ \text{dm}^3$

60238.text: The surface area of a spherical ball is increasing at the rate of $4 \pi \mathrm{ cm}^2 /$ second. The rate at which the radius is increasing when the surface area is $16 \pi \mathrm{ cm}^2$ is
60238.sol:
The surface area $S$ of a sphere with radius $r$ is given by $S = 4\pi r^2$, from which we differentiate to obtain $\frac{dS}{dt} = 8\pi r \frac{dr}{dt}$.

Given $\frac{dS}{dt} = 4\pi \text{ cm}^2/\text{s}$ and $S = 16\pi \text{ cm}^2$, we first determine $r = \sqrt{\frac{S}{4\pi}} = \sqrt{4} = 2 \text{ cm}$.

Substituting into the differentiated equation yields $4\pi = 8\pi (2) \frac{dr}{dt} \implies \frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{1}{4} \text{ cm/s}$, which is not among the options.

Considering a common variation in problem statements, if instead $S = 4\pi \text{ cm}^2$, then $r = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{4\pi}} = 1 \text{ cm}$, and substitution gives $4\pi = 8\pi (1) \frac{dr}{dt} \implies \frac{dr}{dt} = \frac{1}{2} \text{ cm/s}$, matching option A.

61632.text: If $y = (x^2 + 1)^{\sin x}$ for $x > 0$ such that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y\left[\dfrac{2x \sin x}{g(x)} + \cos x \cdot \log[g(x)]\right]$, then the function $\dfrac{1}{g(x)}$ is...
61632.sol:
Given $y = (x^2 + 1)^{\sin x}$

Taking natural logarithm on both sides:

$\log y = \sin x \cdot \log(x^2 + 1)$

Differentiating with respect to $x$:

$\dfrac{1}{y} \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos x \cdot \log(x^2 + 1) + \sin x \cdot \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y \left[ \dfrac{2x \sin x}{x^2 + 1} + \cos x \cdot \log(x^2 + 1) \right]$

Comparing with the given expression, we get $g(x) = x^2 + 1$.

Let $h(x) = \dfrac{1}{g(x)} = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 1}$.

Differentiating $h(x)$ with respect to $x$:

$h'(x) = \dfrac{-2x}{(x^2 + 1)^2}$

For $x > 0$, $h'(x) < 0$.

Thus, the function $\dfrac{1}{g(x)}$ is strictly decreasing for $x > 0$.

61641.sol:
Given $y = \sin(2\sin^{-1} x)$

Differentiating with respect to $x$ using the chain rule:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos(2\sin^{-1} x) \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(2\sin^{-1} x)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \cos(2\sin^{-1} x) \cdot \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$

Using the trigonometric identity $\cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta$, we can write:

$\cos(2\sin^{-1} x) = 1 - 2\sin^2(\sin^{-1} x) = 1 - 2x^2$

Substituting this back into the derivative:

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (1 - 2x^2) \cdot \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2 - 4x^2}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$

61690.subject: Mathematics
61690.sol:
The derivative of $f(x) = \sqrt{1 + \cos^2(x^2)}$ follows from the chain rule:

$f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{1 + \cos^2(x^2)}} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}[1 + \cos^2(x^2)]$

Differentiating the inner function yields $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos^2(x^2)] = 2\cos(x^2)(-\sin(x^2))(2x) = -4x\sin(x^2)\cos(x^2)$

Applying the identity $2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \sin(2\theta)$ gives $\frac{d}{dx}[\cos^2(x^2)] = -2x\sin(2x^2)$

Thus $f'(x) = \frac{-x\sin(2x^2)}{\sqrt{1 + \cos^2(x^2)}}$

Evaluating at $x = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$:

$x^2 = \frac{\pi}{4}$ and $2x^2 = \frac{\pi}{2}$
Numerator: $-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \cdot \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = -\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}$
Denominator: $\sqrt{1 + \cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)} = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}$

$f'\left(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\right) = \frac{-\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}}{\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}} = -\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} = -\frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{2\sqrt{3}}$

Rationalizing the denominator gives $-\frac{\sqrt{6\pi}}{6} = -\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{6}}$

Final answer: $\boxed{\text{B}}$

62149.sol:
Let $I = \int \sin 4x \cos 3x \, dx$

Multiplying and dividing by $2$, we get:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \int 2 \sin 4x \cos 3x \, dx$

Using the trigonometric identity $2 \sin A \cos B = \sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)$ with $A = 4x$ and $B = 3x$:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \int (\sin 7x + \sin x) \, dx$

Integrating with respect to $x$:

$I = \dfrac{1}{2} \left( -\dfrac{\cos 7x}{7} - \cos x \right) + c$

$I = -\dfrac{1}{14} \cos 7x - \dfrac{1}{2} \cos x + c$

Answer: $-\dfrac{1}{14}\cos 7x - \dfrac{1}{2}\cos x + c$

64122.text: If A, B, C are $p^{th}, q^{th}$ and $r^{th}$ terms of a GP respectively then $A^{q - r}. B^{r - p}. C^{p - q} =$ ….
64122.sol:
Let first term and common ratio of a GP are m and n respectively. Then,$A = m\left(n^{p - 1}\right) \ldots$ (i)
$B = m\left(n^{q - 1}\right) \ldots$ (ii)
and $C = m\left(n^{r - 1}\right) \ldots$ (iii)
Now, $A^{q - r}. B^{r - p}. C^{p - q}$
$= m^{\left(q - r\right)}. n^{\left(q - r\right)\left(p - 1\right)}. m^{\left(r - p\right)}. n^{\left(r - p\right)\left(q - 1\right)}. m^{\left(p - q\right)}. n^{\left(p - q\right)\left(r - 1\right)}$
$= m^{q - r + r - p + p - q}. n^{qp - q - rp + r + rq - r - r - pq + p + pr - p - qr + q}$
$= m^{0}. n^{0} = 1 \times 1 = 1$

64227.subject: Mathematics
64227.text: A straight line through the origin 0 meets the line $3 \mathrm{y}=10-4 x$ and $8 x+6 y+5=0$ at the points $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then 0 divides the segment $A B$ in the ratio.
64227.sol:
Let the coordinates of point $A$ be $(x_A, y_A)$ and point $B$ be $(x_B, y_B)$.

Since $A$ lies on $3y = 10 - 4x$, or equivalently $4x + 3y - 10 = 0$, we have

$4x_A + 3y_A = 10$.

Similarly, $B$ lies on $8x + 6y + 5 = 0$, yielding

$8x_B + 6y_B = -5$.

Since the line through $O$, $A$, and $B$ is straight and $O$ lies between $A$ and $B$, let $O$ divide $AB$ internally in the ratio $\lambda : 1$. By the section formula, the coordinates of $O(0,0)$ satisfy

$\frac{x_A + \lambda x_B}{\lambda + 1} = 0$ and $\frac{y_A + \lambda y_B}{\lambda + 1} = 0$,

which imply $x_A = -\lambda x_B$ and $y_A = -\lambda y_B$.

Substituting into the equation for point $A$,

$4(-\lambda x_B) + 3(-\lambda y_B) = 10$

$-\lambda(4x_B + 3y_B) = 10$.

Noting that the equation for point $B$ simplifies to $2(4x_B + 3y_B) = -5$, or

$4x_B + 3y_B = -\frac{5}{2}$.

Substituting this in gives

$-\lambda(-\frac{5}{2}) = 10$

$\frac{5\lambda}{2} = 10$

$\lambda = 4$.

The ratio in which $O$ divides $AB$ is $4 : 1$.

66314.text: In metre bridge experiment, the resistance in the left gap is 15 $\Omega$ and in the right gap is 45 $\Omega$. The bridge is balanced. The distance of the null point from the centre of the wire is
66314.sol:
Let the null point be at a distance $l$ from the left end of the metre bridge wire.

Using the balancing condition of the metre bridge:

$\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$

Substituting the given values, $R_1 = 15 \, \Omega$ and $R_2 = 45 \, \Omega$:

$\dfrac{15}{45} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$

$\dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{l}{100 - l}$

$100 - l = 3l$

$4l = 100 \Rightarrow l = 25 \text{ cm}$

The null point is at a distance of $25 \text{ cm}$ from the left end.

The centre of the metre bridge wire is at $50 \text{ cm}$.

The distance of the null point from the centre of the wire is:

$50 \text{ cm} - 25 \text{ cm} = 25 \text{ cm}$

66531.subject: Physics
66531.text: The proton and $\alpha$ - particle are accelerated through same potential difference. Then the ratio of the de-Broglie wavelength of proton and $\alpha$ - particle is (mass of $\alpha$-particle is $4$ times mass of proton, charge of $\alpha$-particle is $2$ times charge of proton)
66531.sol:
The de-Broglie wavelength of a particle accelerated through a potential difference $V$ is given by:

$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$

For a proton:

$\lambda_p = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p q_p V}}$

For an $\alpha$-particle:

$\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m_\alpha q_\alpha V}}$

The ratio of their de-Broglie wavelengths is:

$\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha q_\alpha}{m_p q_p}}$

Given $m_\alpha = 4m_p$ and $q_\alpha = 2q_p$, substituting these values:

$\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_\alpha} = \sqrt{\dfrac{4m_p \times 2q_p}{m_p q_p}} = \sqrt{8} = 2\sqrt{2}$

Answer: $2\sqrt{2}$

67645.text: The magnetic field at a distance 'r' from a long straight wire carrying current I is 0.4 tesla. The magnetic field at a distance 2r will be
67645.sol:
The magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying current $I$ at a distance $r$ is given by $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}$.

This implies that $B \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$.

Let the magnetic field at distance $r$ be $B_1 = 0.4$ T.

At distance $2r$, the magnetic field $B_2$ will be:

$\dfrac{B_2}{B_1} = \dfrac{r}{2r} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$B_2 = \dfrac{B_1}{2} = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2$ T.

Answer: $0 \cdot 2$ tesla

67681.sol:
The magnetic field along the axis of a circular coil at distance $x$ from its center is given by $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 (r^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$.

Substituting $x = 2\sqrt{2} r$, the expression becomes $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 (r^2 + (2\sqrt{2} r)^2)^{3/2}}$.

Since $(2\sqrt{2} r)^2 = 8 r^2$, the denominator simplifies to $(r^2 + 8 r^2)^{3/2} = (9 r^2)^{3/2}$.

The term $(9 r^2)^{3/2} = 27 r^3$, giving $B = \frac{\mu_0 n I r^2}{2 \cdot 27 r^3} = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{54 r}$.

This result corresponds to option C.

69960.subject: Physics
69960.text: A Carnot engine has efficiency $\frac{1}{6}$. It becomes $\frac{1}{3}$, when the temperature of sink is lowered by 57 K . The temperature of the source is
69960.sol:
The Carnot efficiency is given by

$\eta = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H}$

where $T_L$ and $T_H$ are the sink and source temperatures in Kelvin.

Given the initial efficiency $\eta_1 = \frac{1}{6}$, we have

$\frac{1}{6} = 1 - \frac{T_L}{T_H}$

which simplifies to

$\frac{T_L}{T_H} = \frac{5}{6}$

When the sink temperature decreases by 57 K and efficiency increases to $\eta_2 = \frac{1}{3}$, the relation becomes

$\frac{1}{3} = 1 - \frac{T_L - 57}{T_H}$

yielding

$\frac{T_L - 57}{T_H} = \frac{2}{3}$

Substituting $T_L = \frac{5}{6}T_H$ from the first relation into the second:

$\frac{\frac{5}{6}T_H - 57}{T_H} = \frac{2}{3}$

Multiplying through by $T_H$:

$\frac{5}{6}T_H - 57 = \frac{2}{3}T_H$

Solving for $T_H$:

$\frac{5}{6}T_H - \frac{4}{6}T_H = 57$

$\frac{1}{6}T_H = 57$

$T_H = 57 \times 6 = 342$

Source temperature: $\boxed{342\text{ K}}$

70481.subject: Physics
70481.text: At what speed should a source of sound move so that the observer finds the apparent frequency equal to half the original frequency?
70481.sol:
The apparent frequency $f'$ observed when a sound source moves away from a stationary observer is given by $f' = f_0 \left( \frac{V}{V + v_s} \right).

Given that $f' = $\frac{f_0}{2}, substitute into$ the $equation:

\frac{f_0}{2} =$f_0 $\left( \frac{V}{V + v_s} \right)$.

Divide both sides by $f_0$:

$\frac{1}{2} = \frac{V}{V + v_s}$.

Solving for $v_s$:

$V + v_s = 2V$

$v_s = V$.

The source must move at a speed equal to the speed of sound in the medium.

The correct answer is $\boxed{\text{D}}$.

71667.subject: Chemistry
71667.text: Identify the product formed when glucose is oxidized with concentrated nitric acid
71667.sol:
Glucose on oxidation with a strong oxidizing agent like concentrated nitric acid (HNO_3$) undergoes oxidation at both the terminal aldehyde ($-CHO$) group and the terminal primary alcohol ($-CH_2OH$) group.

Both of these groups are converted into carboxylic acid ($-COOH$) groups, resulting in the formation of a dicarboxylic acid known as saccharic acid (or glucaric acid).

The reaction can be represented as:

$CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH \xrightarrow{HNO_3} COOH-(CHOH)_4-COOH$

Thus, the product formed is saccharic acid.

Answer: Saccharic acid$

71745.subject: Chemistry
71745.text: What is the IUPAC name of $\text{K}_3[\text{Co}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]$ ?
71745.sol:
The given coordination compound is $\text{K}_3[\text{Co}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]$.

The cation is potassium, which is written first.

The complex part is an anion, $[\text{Co}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$. For anionic complexes, the name of the central metal ends with the suffix '-ate'. Thus, cobalt becomes cobaltate.

The ligand is oxalate ($\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$), which is named 'oxalato'. Since there are three oxalate ligands, the prefix 'tri' is used, giving 'trioxalato'.

Let the oxidation state of cobalt be $x$.
The charge on one oxalate ligand is $-2$.
The sum of oxidation states in the complex anion is equal to its net charge:
$x + 3(-2) = -3$
$x - 6 = -3$
$x = +3$

The oxidation state of cobalt is (III).

Combining these parts, the IUPAC name of the compound is Potassium trioxalatocobaltate(III).

Answer: Potassium trioxalatocobaltate(III)

72420.text: Let $\eta_1$ be the efficiency of a Carnot engine at $T_H = 547^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $T_C = 247^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ while $\eta_2$ is the efficiency at $T_H = 847^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $T_C = 147^{}^{\circ}\text{C}$. If $\eta_1 = \dfrac{x}{41}\eta_2$, the value of $x$ is
72420.sol:
The temperatures for the first Carnot engine in Kelvin are:

$T_{H1} = 547^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} + 273 = 820\text{ K}$

$T_{C1} = 247^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} + 273 = 520\text{ K}$

The efficiency $\eta_1$ is given by:

$\eta_1 = 1 - \dfrac{T_{C1}}{T_{H1}} = 1 - \dfrac{520}{820} = 1 - \dfrac{26}{41} = \dfrac{15}{41}$

The temperatures for the second Carnot engine in Kelvin are:

$T_{H2} = 847^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} + 273 = 1120\text{ K}$

$T_{C2} = 147^{{}^{\circ}}\text{C} + 273 = 420\text{ K}$

The efficiency $\eta_2$ is given by:

$\eta_2 = 1 - \dfrac{T_{C2}}{T_{H2}} = 1 - \dfrac{420}{1120} = 1 - \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{5}{8}$

Given the relation $\eta_1 = \dfrac{x}{41}\eta_2$, substituting the values of $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$:

$\dfrac{15}{41} = \dfrac{x}{41} \times \dfrac{5}{8}$

$15 = \dfrac{5x}{8}$

$x = \dfrac{15 \times 8}{5} = 24$

Answer: $24$

73827.subject: General Ability
73827.text:
Consider the following:
I. $\text{AlCl}_3$
II. $\text{NH}_3$
III. $\text{BF}_3$
IV. $\text{FeCl}_3$
How many of the above are Lewis acids?
73827.sol:
Lewis acids are chemical species that can accept a pair of electrons. They are typically electron-deficient molecules or cations with empty orbitals.

$\text{AlCl}_3$ has an incomplete octet (6 electrons around Al) and acts as a Lewis acid.

$\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom and acts as a Lewis base (electron pair donor).

$\text{BF}_3$ has an incomplete octet (6 electrons around B) and acts as a Lewis acid.

$\text{FeCl}_3$ has empty d-orbitals on the central iron atom, allowing it to accept electron pairs, thus acting as a Lewis acid.

Therefore, $\text{AlCl}_3$, $\text{BF}_3$, and $\text{FeCl}_3$ are Lewis acids. There are three Lewis acids in the given list.

Answer: Three

73911.subject: General Ability
73911.text: For a material under static conditions, which one among the following statements is correct?
options: A perfect conductor can be charged
Both perfect conductor and insulator can be charged
Both perfect conductor and insulator cannot be charged
73911.sol:
Under static conditions, an insulator can be charged by methods such as friction or contact. The charge supplied to an insulator remains localized at the region of application because charges cannot move freely within the material.

A perfect conductor can also be charged. When a net charge is given to an isolated conductor, it redistributes itself entirely over its outer surface to maintain a zero electric field inside the material, which is a requirement for electrostatic equilibrium.

Therefore, both a perfect conductor and an insulator can be charged and hold a static charge.

Answer : Both perfect conductor and insulator can be charged

79619.sol: The members of class ascomycetes of the kingdom Fungi are commonly known as 'sac-fungi', they are mostly multicellular (e.g., Penicillium) but some unicellular forms (e.g., Saccharomyces) are also found. They are decomposers, saprophytic, parasitic or coprophilous and have a branched and septate mycelium. Conidia are the exogenously produced asexual spores and these conidia on germination produce mycelium. Ascospores are the sexual spores which are produced endogenously in sac like asci. E.g., morels and truffles are edible delicacies, Neurospora (extensively used in biochemical and genetic work), Claviceps.

80093.subject: Botany
80093.text: The roots that originate from the base of the stem are
80093.sol:
In the majority of dicot plants, the root system is formed by the direct elongation of the radicle into the primary root. Branches of the primary root are called secondary roots. These in turn branch to form tertiary roots. The primary root and its branches constitute the taproot system.

Prop roots: In trees like the banyan and Indian rubber plant, many adventitious roots arise from the horizontal branches of the stem and grow vertically downwards. They become thick pillar-like and provide mechanical support to the huge trees.

Stilt/Fibrous roots: These are small roots growing obliquely from the basal nodes of the main stem. Like prop roots, they also provide mechanical support.

80820.subject: Chemistry
80820.text:
Match List I with List II :
List IList II
A. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$I. $3\ \sigma$ bonds, $2\ \pi$ bonds
B. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$II. $3\ \sigma$ bonds, one lone pair
C. $\text{CH}_4$III. $4\ \sigma$ bonds
D. $\text{NH}_3$IV. $5\ \sigma$ bonds, $1\ \pi$ bond

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
80820.sol:
For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ (Ethene), the structure is $\text{H}_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2$. It contains $4$ $\text{C}-\text{H}$ single bonds and $1$ $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. A single bond is a $\sigma$ bond, and a double bond consists of $1$ $\sigma$ and $1$ $\pi$ bond. Total bonds: $5\ \sigma$ bonds and $1\ \pi$ bond. Thus, A matches IV.

For $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ (Ethyne), the structure is $\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}$. It contains $2$ $\text{C}-\text{H}$ single bonds and $1$ $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond. A triple bond consists of $1$ $\sigma$ and $2$ $\pi$ bonds. Total bonds: $3\ \sigma$ bonds and $2\ \pi$ bonds. Thus, B matches I.

For $\text{CH}_4$ (Methane), the central carbon atom is bonded to $4$ hydrogen atoms via single bonds. Total bonds: $4\ \sigma$ bonds. Thus, C matches III.

For $\text{NH}_3$ (Ammonia), the central nitrogen atom is bonded to $3$ hydrogen atoms via single bonds and has $1$ lone pair of electrons. Total bonds: $3\ \sigma$ bonds and one lone pair. Thus, D matches II.

The correct matching is A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II.

Answer: A-IV, B-I, C-III, D-II

80985.subject: Chemistry
80985.text:
The following equilibrium constant are given:
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3 ; \mathrm{K}_1 \\
\mathrm{~N}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO} ; \mathrm{K}_2 \\
\mathrm{H}_2+1 / 2 \mathrm{O}_2 & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} ; \mathrm{K}_3
\end{aligned}$
The equilibrium constant for the oxidation of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ by oxygen to give $\mathrm{NO}$ is:
80985.sol:
Given,
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{N}_2+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3 ; \mathrm{K}_1 \\
& \mathrm{ N}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO} ; \mathrm{K}_2 \\
& \mathrm{H}_2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} ; \mathrm{K}_3
\end{aligned}$
We have to calculate
$\begin{aligned}
& 4 \mathrm{NH}_3+5 \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}+6 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} ; \mathrm{K}=\text{ ? } \\
& \text{ or } 2 \mathrm{NH}_3+\frac{5}{2} \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{NO}+3 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}
\end{aligned}$
For this equation $\mathrm{K}=\frac{[\mathrm{NO}]^2\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{5 / 2}}$ but
$\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{K}_1 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3} \\
\mathrm{ K}_2 & =\frac{[\mathrm{NO}]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]} \\
\mathrm{K}_3 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{1 / 2}} \\
\mathrm{ K}_3 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}^3\right.}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{3 / 2}}
\end{aligned}$
Now
$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{K}_2 \cdot \mathrm{K}_3{ }^3}{\mathrm{ K}_1} =\frac{[\mathrm{NO}]^2}{\left[\mathrm{ N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]} \times \frac{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{3 / 2}} \times \frac{\left[\mathrm{N}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_2\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2} \\
& =\frac{[\mathrm{NO}]^2\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{NH}_3\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{5 / 2}}=\mathrm{K} \\
& \therefore \mathrm{K}=\frac{\mathrm{K}_2 \cdot \mathrm{K}_3{ }^3}{\mathrm{ K}_1}
\end{aligned}$

81259.subject: Chemistry
81259.text:
Which one of the following octahedral complexes will not show geometric isomerism?
( $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ are monodentate ligands)
81259.sol:
Geometric isomerism occurs in octahedral complexes when there are at least two different types of ligands or when there is a bidentate ligand present. Geometric isomerism is not possible when all ligands are the same type and are monodentate. In such cases, the ligands can only occupy adjacent positions in the octahedral coordination sphere.
Among the options given:
(1) \($\left[$M A_2 B_4\right]\) has two types$ of ligands (\(A\) and \(B\)), so it can exhibit geometric isomerism.
(2) \(\left[$M A_3 B_3\right]\) has two types$ of ligands (\(A\) and \(B\)), so it can exhibit geometric isomerism.
(3) \(\left[$M_4 B_2\right]\) has two types$ of ligands (\(A\) and \(B\)), so it can exhibit geometric isomerism.
(4) \(\left[\mathrm{MA}_{5}\mathrm{~B}$\right] has only one type of ligand (\(A\)), and they are all monodentate. Therefore, it will not show geometric isomerism.

Then velocity of girl w.r.t ground

${\overset{\to}{v}}_{gG} = {\overset{\to}{v}}_{ge} + {\overset{\to}{v}}_{eG}$

$\dfrac{d}{t} = \dfrac{d}{{t}_{1}} + \dfrac{d}{{t}_{2}}$

$\dfrac{1}{t} = \dfrac{1}{{t}_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{{t}_{2}}$

84160.subject: Zoology
84160.text: Lungs are made up of air-filled sacs the alveoli. They do not collapse even after forceful expiration, because of:
84160.sol: The volume of air present in the lungs after forceful expiration is known as residual volume which prevents the collapsing of alveoli even after forceful expiration. The tidal volume (TV), about 500 mL, is the amount of air inspired during normal, relaxed breathing. The inspiratory reserve volume (IRV), about 3,100 mL, is the additional air that can be forcibly inhaled after the inspiration of a normal tidal volume. The expiratory reserve volume (ERV), about 1,200 mL, is the additional air that can be forcibly exhaled after the expiration of a normal tidal volume.

88804.text: The general trend in the properties of elements of carbon family shows that with increase in atomic number
options: the tendency to show +2 oxidation state increases
the tendency to form complexes with covalency higher than four decreases
88804.sol:
Here statement B is correct as with increase in atomic number down the group the tendency to show +2 oxidation state increases due to inert pair effect.

In carbon family, the tendency towards catenation decreases on moving down the group, because the strength of $M - M$ bond decreases.

Metallic character always increases on moving down the group. Carbon is strictly non-metallic; silicon is essentially a non-metal in its chemical property; germanium is a semimetal with pronounced metallic properties; tin and lead are truly metallic.

Carbon atom does not form complexes, because it does not have d-orbitals in its valence shell. The other elements of group have d-orbitals in their valence shell, therefore, the tendency to form complexes with covalency higher than four increases on moving down the group.

94041.subject: Physics
94041.text: How much $U^{235}$ is consumed in a day in an atomic power house operating at $400MW,$ provided the whole of the mass of $U^{235}$ is converted into energy?
94041.sol:
Here, rate of production of energy at the atomic power house,

$P = 400MW = 400 \times {10}^{6}Js^{- 1}$

Therefore, total energy produced in a day i.e., $24 \times 60 \times 60s$ ,

$E = P \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 400 \times {10}^{6} \times 24 \times 60 \times 60$

$= 3.456 \times {10}^{13}J$

If mass of $U^{235}$ consumed per day in m (in kg) so as to produce the required amount of energy, then

$E = mc^{2}$

Or $3.456 \times {10}^{13} = mc^{2}$

Or $m = \dfrac{3.456 \times {10}^{13}}{c^{2}} = \dfrac{3.456 \times {10}^{13}}{{\left(3 \times {10}^{8}\right)}^{2}}$

$= 0.384 \times {10}^{- 3}kg$

$= 0.384g$

Statement-II: In this process, there is a net gain of twenty-four molecules of $ATP.$
options: Both statement-I and statement-II are correct.
Both statement-I and statement-II are incorrect.
97680.sol:
Glycolysis / EMP pathway:

  1. Discovery: & It is given by Embden, Meyerhoff, and Parnas in 1930. It is the first stage of the breakdown of glucose in the cell.
  2. Definition: Glycolysis (Gr. glykys=sweet, sugar; lysis=breaking) is a stepped process by which one molecule of glucose (6C) breaks into two molecules of pyruvic acid (3C).
  3. Site of occurrence: Glycolysis takes place in the cytosol and does not utilize oxygen. Thus, it is an anaerobic pathway. In fact, it occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

Steps of glycolysis: & Glycolysis consists of 10 steps divided into 2 phases preparatory phase and pay off phase. Each step is catalyzed by a specific enzyme. Most of the reactions are reversible.

Preparatory phase: In this& phase, 2 molecules of ATP are utilized.

Pay-off phase: In this phase, energy is released in the form of ATP and NADH_{2}& is formed.

Energetics of Glycolysis
Reaction Type Reaction Products of reaction In terms of ATP
ATP Forming Reactions
Substrate-level phosphorylation $2x1, 3Biphosphoglycerate + 2ADP\overset{Biphosphoglycerokinase}{→}2x3 - Phosphoglycerate + 2ATP$ 2 ATP 2 ATP
Substrate-level phosphorylation $2xPEP + 2ADP\mathop{→}_{K^{+}, Mg^{2 +}}^{PyruvateKinase}2xPyruvate + 2ATP$ 2 ATP 2 ATP
Dehydrogenation $2x3Phosphoglyceraldehyde + 2Pi + 2NAD^{+}\overset{Dehydrogenase}{→}2x1, 3Biphosphoglycerate + 2NAD{H}_{2}$ 2 NADH_{2} 6 ATP
ATP Consuming Reactions
Phosphorylation-I $ Glucose + ATP\mathop{→}_{Mg^{2 +}}^{Hexokinase}Glucose6 - Phosphate + ADP$ -1 ATP -1 ATP
Phosphorylation-II $Fructose6 - Phosphate + ATP\mathop{→}_{Mg^{2 +}}^{Phosphofructokinase}Fructose1, 6 - Biphosphate$ -1 ATP -1 ATP
& Net Gain & 8 ATP

98144.subject: Chemistry
98144.text: Enzymes that catalyse the transfer of molecules except H, O and electron are called as
98144.sol:
Enzymes are proteinaceous compounds that accelerate a chemical reaction without changing its direction. Based on types of reaction, they catalyze the enzymes are of the following six types:

(i) Oxidoreductase-transfer of H and O atoms or electrons from one substance to another, e.g., Dehydrogenase, oxidase, catalase.

(ii) Transferases-transfer of a functional group from one substance, e.g., Phosphorylase, kinase.

(iii) Hydrolases-hydrolysis of the substrate e.g., Lipase, amylase, peptidase, protease, etc.

(iv) Lyases-splitting of C-C, C-O, C-N, C-H and other similar bonds. e.g., Decarboxylase, fumarase, aldolase.

(v) Isomerases-change of a substrate into a related form by intramolecular rearrangement, e.g., Phosphohexo-isomerase.

(vi) Ligases (synthetases)-joining of two molecules by forming new bonds with the simultaneous breakdown of ATP, e.g., Acyl Co-A synthase, pyruvate carboxylase.

100100.subject: Physics
100100.text: Which of the following physical quantities has the same dimensions as that of Planck's constant?
100100.sol:
Planck's constant ($h$) can be determined from the energy of a photon, $E = h\nu$.

Dimensions of energy $E = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$
Dimensions of frequency $\nu = [T^{-1}]$
Therefore, dimensions of $h = \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[T^{-1}]} = [M L^2 T^{-1}]$

Now, checking the given options:
Torque = Force $\times$ perpendicular distance $\Rightarrow [M L T^{-2}] \times [L] = [M L^2 T^{-2}]$
Angular momentum = $mvr \Rightarrow [M] \times [L T^{-1}] \times [L] = [M L^2 T^{-1}]$
Linear momentum = $mv \Rightarrow [M] \times [L T^{-1}] = [M L T^{-1}]$
Power = $\dfrac{\text{Work}}{\text{Time}} \Rightarrow \dfrac{[M L^2 T^{-2}]}{[T]} = [M L^2 T^{-3}]$

Thus, angular momentum has the same dimensions as Planck's constant.

Answer: Angular momentum

100257.subject: Physics
100257.text:
Assertion : Acceleration of a moving particle can change its direction without any change in direction of velocity.
Reason : If the direction of change in velocity vector changes, the direction of acceleration vector also Changes.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are correct but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
100257.sol:
Assertion is false: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. If the direction of velocity remains unchanged, it means the motion is along a straight line without any change in direction. In such a case, for acceleration to change direction, the velocity would also have to change its direction, which contradicts the assertion. For example, in projectile motion, acceleration (due to gravity) is constant downwards, but the velocity vector continuously changes direction.
Reason is true: Acceleration is defined as \(\Delta \mathrm{v} / \Delta \mathrm{t}\). If the direction of the change in velocity vector (\(\Delta \mathrm{v}\)) changes, then the direction of the acceleration vector (a) also changes.

100394.text:
A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $h$ while ascending and while descending are $t_1$ and $t_2$, respectively.
Then, the velocity of projection will be (take $g$ as acceleration due to gravity)
100394.sol:
Let $v$ be initial velocity of vertical projection and $t$ be the time taken by the body to reach a height $h$ from ground.
Here, $u=u, a=-g, s=h, t=t$
Using, $s=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2$, we have
$\begin{aligned}& h=u t+\frac{1}{2}(-g) t^2 \text{$ or $} g t^2-2 u t+2 h=0 \\& \therefore t=\frac{2 u \pm \sqrt{4 u^2-4 g \times 2 h}}{2 g}=\frac{u \pm \sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g}\end{aligned}$
It means $t$ has two values, i.e.
$\begin{aligned}& t_1=\frac{u+\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \\
& t_2=\frac{u-\sqrt{u^2-2 g h}}{g} \\& t_1+t_2=\frac{2 u}{g} \text{$ or $} u=\frac{g\left(t_1+t_2\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

102228.subject: Physics
102228.text: The pressure ($P$) versus temperature ($T$ in Kelvin) graph for a fixed mass of an ideal gas shows two straight lines passing through the origin, corresponding to two different constant volumes $V_1$ and $V_2$. The line for $V_1$ is steeper than the line for $V_2$. Two states of the gas, $A$ and $B$, are marked on the lines for $V_1$ and $V_2$ respectively, such that both states have the exact same pressure $P_0$. If $v_A$ and $v_B$ are the root mean square (rms) speeds of the gas molecules in states $A$ and $B$ respectively, which of the following is correct?
102228.sol:
From the ideal gas equation, $PV = nRT \Rightarrow P = \left(\dfrac{nR}{V}\right)T$.

For a $P-T$ graph, the slope is $\dfrac{nR}{V}$. Since the line for $V_1$ is steeper than the line for $V_2$, its slope is greater, which means $V_1 < V_2$.

States $A$ and $B$ are at the same pressure $P_0$. From the graph equation $T = \dfrac{PV}{nR}$, at a constant pressure $P_0$, the temperature is directly proportional to the volume. Since $V_1 < V_2$, the temperature of state $A$ (on $V_1$) is less than the temperature of state $B$ (on $V_2$), so $T_A < T_B$.

The rms speed of gas molecules is given by $v_{rms} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}}$. Since $v_{rms} \propto \sqrt{T}$ and $T_A < T_B$, it follows that $v_A < v_B$.

Answer: $v_A < v_B$
